title: Knowledge Check: Reliability, Scalability, and Load

questions.prompt: A disk dies in one database server, but a replica takes over and every request still succeeds. How do you describe what happened?
options: A failure, but not a fault
A fault that didn't become a failure
Both a fault and a failure
Neither: nothing went wrong

questions.prompt: When Twitter moved to pushing each tweet into followers' cached timelines, which load parameter turned out to matter most?
options: The average length of a tweet
The number of tweets posted per second
The distribution of followers per user
The number of data centers serving reads

questions.prompt: A service's p99 response time is 1.5 seconds. What does that mean?
options: 1 in 100 requests takes at least 1.5 seconds
99% of requests take about 1.5 seconds
The average request takes 1.5 seconds
The single slowest request took 1.5 seconds

questions.prompt: Why is the mean a poor summary of response times?
options: It's expensive to compute over millions of requests
It's always higher than the median
It ignores the fastest requests
It doesn't tell you how many users actually experienced a delay

questions.prompt: Loading one page makes 10 backend calls in parallel. Each backend is slow (beyond its p99) on 1% of calls. Roughly what fraction of page loads are slow?
options: About 0.1%
About 1%
About 10%
About 99%

questions.prompt: Strictly speaking, how does latency differ from response time?
options: They're two names for the same measurement
Latency is the time a request spends waiting to be handled; response time is everything the client sees
Latency includes network delays, and response time doesn't
Response time is measured by the server, latency by the client

questions.prompt: A server's utilization climbs from 50% to 95% as traffic grows. What happens to response times?
options: They rise steeply, because queues form and grow faster near full capacity
They rise in exact proportion to the traffic
They stay flat until utilization reaches 100%
They fall, because caches stay warmer under load

questions.prompt: Which part of a system is the hardest to scale out across many machines?
options: Stateless API servers behind a load balancer
Static files such as images and scripts
Data: databases and other stateful components
The load balancer itself

questions.prompt: A team adds clear dashboards, predictable behavior, and sane defaults so on-call engineers can keep the system healthy. Which maintainability principle is that?
options: Simplicity
Evolvability
Elasticity
Operability
